tweets.text:
Advanced Micro Devices ($AMD) shares up 8% after a Q3 beat and guiding Q4 well above the Street on data center strength.

Third quarter vs. TipRanks consensus:
▪️ Non-GAAP EPS $2.09 vs. $1.95, up 74% from a year ago
▪️ Revenue $13.38B vs. $13.1B, up 45%, and $77M above the top of AMD’s own guide range
▪️ Data Center a record $8.55B, up 97%, vs. $8.2B expected per Bloomberg
▪️ Client $2.95B, up 7%, a hair under the $3.0B FactSet estimate
▪️ Gaming $773M, down 40% but well above the $634M estimate; Embedded $1.11B, up 29%

Fourth-quarter guide: $17B, plus or minus 3%, vs. $16.14B consensus. Even the low end beats by about $350M. The non-GAAP gross margin guide of about 55% though is down from 56%; StreetAccount was at 55.3%, per CNBC but markets seem to be looking past that.

Data Center added $4.2B, 102% of AMD’s $4.1B revenue increase. Everything else combined shrank 1.5%. Data Center now earns 74% of segment operating income on 64% of revenue, and its operating margin rose 9 points to 33.7%.

Some other quibbles:
▪️ Free cash flow fell 64% to $554M, about half the $1.05B expected and a 4% margin vs. 17% a year ago, as working capital absorbed $3.4B. The biggest piece was a $3.0B inventory build; inventory is up 45% since December to $11.5B.
▪️ No buybacks. AMD spent $1.5B withholding employee shares for taxes, 2.7 times free cash flow, and borrowed $4.7B.
▪️ GAAP EPS of $1.46 absorbed a $1.1B charge on warrants issued to customers. That liability rises with the share price.

The hyperscaler math: Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta spent $208.8B on capex last quarter. AMD’s Data Center revenue was 4.1% of that, so each point of share is worth about $2.1B a quarter.

To watch: fourth-quarter cash flow, inventory, and the margin step-down.

Netflix had a slide in its original culture deck that said "adequate performance gets a generous severance package."  

Reed Hastings explains why Netflix paid 4-9 months severance packages and how the Keeper Test worked:  

"One of the best things is to do large severance packages like four to nine months of salary. It feels expensive at first, but it makes the person who's let go feel better because they've got a bunch of money in their pocket. 

Two, it helps the manager do their job because then they don't feel as bad in letting the person go.   

It's like a professional sports player. The test that we encourage people to use is, if someone were quitting, would you try to keep them.    

Honestly, if you quit, I wouldn't try to change your mind to stay. The reason is I think I could get someone in your role that could do what you're doing plus even more, and here's why."

Andrew Huberman says Rick Rubin knows exactly when his mind is sharpest, and the two of them are trying to build tools to unlock that focus more quickly and deeply:

"My friend Rick Rubin... his work block generally is in the afternoon. That's when his mind is sharpest, and then he tapers off in the evening. But he's working extremely hard in those hours, and he knows when those fall."

"If you're in one of those windows and you allow your attention to be captured by something that's not worthwhile... the productivity that comes in those three or four hours is exponentially greater than the productivity that comes from doing that work at some point later."

"We don't really have formal protocols for task switching, but this is extremely important for company founders and employees across the board, right?"

"Rick and I have been kicking around some tools that are not meditations... that would allow you to kind of program your mind for what comes next."

"If you think about it, it's 2026. Why in the world are we sitting down to do work and just going, 'Okay, now I'm gonna be focused, and now I'm gonna be creative.'"

"We should have ways to control neural activity that would allow us to access those circuits more quickly and more deeply."

@hubermanlab

LLMs had the entire internet to learn from. Robots have no equivalent. Nobody is recording data like the pressure in their fingertips when they pick up a coffee cup.

Tutor Intelligence is building that dataset. Its robots work real shifts in factories and warehouses across 20 US states, from mom-and-pop shops to Fortune 50 companies, and have helped make and ship more than 250 million products.

Tutor hires out robots by the hour. When one gets stuck, a remote human "tutor" takes over and guides it through the task, and that becomes training data that makes the whole fleet smarter. (Hence the name.)

The 160-person team trains its own robot models, builds its own robots, and ships code to them every day. The fleet has grown 4x since last year, and Tutor just raised a $75M Series B led by a16z.

Co-founder and CEO Josh Gruenstein:

"I think it's one of the only places in the universe where you can be on a whiteboard talking about model architecture in the morning, and in the afternoon, looking at a factory line."

Tutor is hiring across robotics research, software, hardware, and operations in Boston and SF: https://t.co/gNulNs5mM9

@joshgruenstein @tutorintel

thread_tweets.text:
EDR is basically just anomaly detection, and I don't think that's true at all. At the end of the day, having active monitoring on your own computer to see "is there weird thing happening in sensitive directories that shouldn't be happening" is a solved problem.

In this case for DevOps engineers, I guarantee you that going forward, they will not be able to run ANY binaries that are not approved by IT. In which case this category of attack will no longer be possible. And any machine that writes to pyenv or hooks into random .dlls will suddenly get taken offline.

A lot of this stuff gets calibrated based on employees complaining "this is annoying, it's too sensitive, it's too trigger-happy, I can't do my job." After you get hacked for billions, you stop caring about that and default to extremely aggressive settings for your org.

Security everywhere is like this, and I bet that's a lot of the takeaway for Binance internally.

Andrew Huberman on the best advice he ever got: figure out the most real work you can do every day, consistently, and find a way to reset every week.

"The best advice I ever got: there was a neurologist out at UC Berkeley and UCSF, Bob Knight, some years ago, very talented. I asked him for advice starting graduate school."

"He said, 'Figure out the maximum amount of real work that you can do every day consistently, and then figure out some non-destructive way to reset yourself every single week.'"

"I said, 'How do you reset?' He said he likes fishing. I like to hike. I like to get into nature and spend time with people while I do it. I figured out I could work X number of hours per day, 5 days a week, and I just stuck to it for 25 years."

"People who take a ton of stimulants and just blitz, blitz, blitz, blitz, blitz. These are the same people that crash and disappear. You have to figure out and build your capacity."

"Yes, you have to work extremely hard. You have to be extremely focused. But you also have to figure out how long you can keep this up."

@hubermanlab

It's officially election day.

History says stocks are heading higher.

In fact, the S&P 500 has closed GREEN in the year following every US Midterm election since 1980.

As we noted in our analysis yesterday, we believe recent weakness in markets is largely a function of the uncertainty around Midterm elections.

However, when this uncertainty dissipates, markets react positively.

Since 1980, the S&P 500 has averaged a +14% gain in the 12 months following US Midterm elections.

Furthermore, even after divided-government outcomes, the index has averaged a +15% one-year gain, compared to +12% under single-party control.

Of course, the near-term picture will come with volatility and change.

But, if history is any guide, it's a great time to be bullish.

Turn on our post notifications at @KobeissiLetter for real-time analysis as this develops.

Furthermore, the S&P 500 Semiconductors & Semiconductor Equipment Index fell more than -5% on 12 trading days over the last 5 months.

The index is now down -32% from its June peak, trading at its lowest level since April.

Semiconductor stocks are experiencing historic volatility.

Many of the power plants being built for AI do not show up in official data.

Official energy statistics only track plants tied to the grid, so much of what AI campuses build on site goes uncounted. 

Plants like these are expected to power more than half of the new U.S. data center capacity coming online in 2028.

Builders are bringing their own power because the grid cannot connect new load fast enough. One off-grid campus in Texas alone plans more than 500 gas engines.

Engine makers’ order books show the buildout more clearly than the official data does. INNIO booked $6.1 billion of orders in the first nine months of 2026, nearly double a year earlier. 

Caterpillar’s backlog of large engines has more than tripled since early 2024, and Wärtsilä’s energy orders have more than doubled since early 2025.

These plants are likely to stay after the grid arrives. Some providers now build and run them for data centers under contracts that last up to 18 years, including extensions. 

A growing share of AI’s power now comes from plants beside the grid, many of them outside the official numbers.

even though I've been rooting for Aerodrome to keep gaining overall DEX market share lately, I have nothing but the highest respect for Uniswap.

incredible how they've almost single-handedly kept eating market share from CEXs, now sitting at more than 31% of Binance's spot volume.

we don't get a ton of success stories like this in crypto. but it's exactly these rare cases of real innovation that keep me going, regardless of bull or bear market.

incredible what we can build as an industry despite all the obstacles in our way. and long term, it's always good to be reminded that the good ones win.

love to see it, true inspiration for all builders out there that genuinely care about building something long lasting. the better product will always win, regardless how intimidating your competition and incumbents may look like.

job isn't done until we're at 100%.

tweets.text:
so I fundamentally disagree with this take. 

it's important we discuss it in light of the Brazil election being mispriced, and potentially some big prediction market misses today in the midterms (we will see). 

first of all, can a prediction market be wrong? yes. a PM can be mispriced relative to the "true" probability. 

was the 80c price for Bolso ahead of the election "wrong"? yes. the polls showed a dead heat. the market on the PM was showing tons of conviction the wrong way around. 80 cents was wrong. 

saying "20c odds happen one in five times so 20c was not wrong" is unfalsifiable. a PM can never be mispriced according to that logic. 

second, electoral PMs are not the same as dice rolls or other sources of "genuine" randomness. 

elections are uncertain in the epistemic sense - it's hard to gather all the data beforehand and price them. this is not the same kind of uncertainty you get from rolling a fair die. unlike the die, there is always some kind of inherent underlying political reality to be discovered. 

the "true probability" of an election given perfect knowledge is going to be 100/0 one way. of course, no one has perfect knowledge, which is in theory the value prop of PMs; giving sharps the financial incentive to go out there and discover that knowledge and furnish it in the form of prices. 

it's not reasonable to say "underdogs sometimes win, so a 20c probability that happens is automatically valid". you could use that to justify any nonzero probability even down to 0.1c. 

elections are not card draws or dice rolls. they are events that condense political realities into a single number. PMs are meant to pay people to discover that number. the PM in the case of Brazil (and maybe the midterms – who knows) failed to do this. so the PM was "wrong", in the sense that it wasn't useful. in fact, it was was actively worse than what the polls were suggesting. that makes it wrong.

Lula's upset in Brazil's runoff election is pointed to as proof prediction markets don't offer accurate signal. This take misses the mark.

tweets.full_text:
so I fundamentally disagree with this take. 

it's important we discuss it in light of the Brazil election being mispriced, and potentially some big prediction market misses today in the midterms (we will see). 

first of all, can a prediction market be wrong? yes. a PM can be mispriced relative to the "true" probability. 

was the 80c price for Bolso ahead of the election "wrong"? yes. the polls showed a dead heat. the market on the PM was showing tons of conviction the wrong way around. 80 cents was wrong. 

saying "20c odds happen one in five times so 20c was not wrong" is unfalsifiable. a PM can never be mispriced according to that logic. 

second, electoral PMs are not the same as dice rolls or other sources of "genuine" randomness. 

elections are uncertain in the epistemic sense - it's hard to gather all the data beforehand and price them. this is not the same kind of uncertainty you get from rolling a fair die. unlike the die, there is always some kind of inherent underlying political reality to be discovered. 

the "true probability" of an election given perfect knowledge is going to be 100/0 one way. of course, no one has perfect knowledge, which is in theory the value prop of PMs; giving sharps the financial incentive to go out there and discover that knowledge and furnish it in the form of prices. 

it's not reasonable to say "underdogs sometimes win, so a 20c probability that happens is automatically valid". you could use that to justify any nonzero probability even down to 0.1c. 

elections are not card draws or dice rolls. they are events that condense political realities into a single number. PMs are meant to pay people to discover that number. the PM in the case of Brazil (and maybe the midterms – who knows) failed to do this. so the PM was "wrong", in the sense that it wasn't useful. in fact, it was was actively worse than what the polls were suggesting. that makes it wrong.

This is JP Morgan’s view is Wall Street consensus. It assumes there is one Democratic Party. 

My view aligns more with Democrat Strategist Jim Carville, who spoke on the Bulwark podcast two weeks ago. He suggests there are two Democratic parties, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and the more moderate/traditional Democrats. These divisions mean the margin of victory might play a huge role in the market’s reaction.
--
Carville:
“I would be disappointed if it comes in at 225 House seats. That would almost be—I would rather the Republicans keep the House by five than the Democrats win by five because if that happens, they’re hostage to the DSA. Like, Hakeem [Jeffries] cannot move. He has nowhere to go. Even if you have a close Senate, [Sen. John] Fetterman would keep [Sen. Chuck] Schumer Pepto-Bismol all night. So I think this is one of those races where margin matters a lot.”
--

We would add that if the Senate is a 51-49 Democrat majority, not only does presumed Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer have to worry about PA Senator John Fetterman siding with Republicans, but Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders and a presumed Michigan winner Abdul El-Sayed could put up a “block” because the Democratic Party is not progressive enough.

This issue would come to a head almost immediately over data centers.

Moderate/traditional Democrats, such as unions and middle-class voters, want those jobs. They are accelerationists. 

The DSA wants to block more data center construction. They are decelerationists.

This could turn into an epic fight within the Democratic Party.

We have turned a page on Iran. Again. And this time the data agrees with me.

I have called the end of this war more than once this year, so a little humility is in order. But in late March, when Brent was at its highs and the consensus was “one more spike,” the Nowcast IQ data told us something different: the physical gauges were calm, the inflation impulse was peaking, and positioning was crowded long oil. We said the page was turning. Within six weeks Brent had lost $25 and the AI trade had its best run of the year.

Here is what the data shows now, and why it rhymes.

Oil futures are back at 51-52% net long of open interest, exactly where they were in March. The VLCC rates from the Gulf have rolled over. The 321 cracks have dropped, gasoline leading. The Houston export spread is back near a dollar against $7 in the spring. Nobody is bidding up the marginal barrel.

And on Monday the Supreme Leader gave the government “certain authorities” to negotiate. Brent fell 8%.

Meanwhile the US growth nowcast has turned from 19% to 34% since late September. It led the April rally by six weeks last time. The inflation breadth measure fell while the headline rose, and the Fed and the ECB both backed off versus what the market had pencilled in.

Oil down, growth turning, inflation momentum peaking, positioning wrong-footed. That is the March setup, with the dates moved.

I do not know if the Ayatollah means it this time. I know what the data says, and I know what it said last time.

$WYFI announced acquisition of NC2 and NC3 sites in North Carolina closed for $60M in cash. 
Expected to provide a miniumum of 60MWs of initial gross capacity with potential up to 200MWs, with initial RFS in late 2027. IR said previously they were targeting 3Q27 and now saying late 2027 so appears relatively in-line (this could be leased any time now we think). The PR says that development spending plans are expected to be aligned with definitive customer agreements and financing (they are looking to sign customer and raise debt backed by them at the same time to avoid similar Nscale situation).
Looks like the seller is continuing to occupy part of the building, which will offset a portion of property carrying costs as WYFI advances dev plans (good way for WYFI to save some money until lease starts).
They also said that NC1 billing didn't hit the full target in August, but now 35MW of the 40MW are running, and they are still within initial budget with capital investment "substantially complete" - this is later/worse date then expected, but good that the spending is nearly done (3Q and 4Q revs to be lighter than expected)
Still working on financing for NC1.

💸🗳️Affordability will be one of the biggest issues on voters’ minds today.

And while we wait for the vote counts to start coming in, our colleagues at @economics just released a fascinating new way to look at it: the Bloomberg Price Project.

It uses millions of alternative-data price points to break inflation down into nearly 700 categories — more than 3x the detail of the official CPI.

And maybe best of all, the full dataset is available to all Bloomberg Terminal clients via ECAN US BPI <GO>.

The big picture: inflation is still too high, but the pressure looks much less broad-based than it did in 2022. A relatively narrow group of categories — particularly energy and AI-exposed goods — is doing much of the heavy lifting.

And at least one bit of relief at the grocery store: the surge in beef prices appears to be reversing. 🥩📉

A very cool dataset to explore — read more about it here, and dig deeper on ECAN US BPI <GO>: 
https://t.co/yy7FfxjswX

$ZIM: 𝐒𝐡𝐨𝐰 𝐌𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐲

Market Cap: ~$3.5 billion
Share Price: ~$28.20
Expected Year-End Cash: ~$32/share
Book Value per Share: ~$50/share
Margin of Safety: HIGH

For those new to $ZIM, it is an Israeli container shipping company. Hapag-Lloyd agreed to acquire it for $35 per share. We believe the deal will fail, and we hope it does.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐀𝐜𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧

Israel’s golden share gives the government special rights over $ZIM. The original acquisition structure faced serious government objections over Israel’s strategic shipping interests.

Hapag-Lloyd partnered with FIMI, an Israeli private equity fund, to address these concerns through the transfer of certain ships and operations to an Israeli-controlled company, along with employee protections.

We estimate the total economic cost to Hapag-Lloyd could reach approximately $49 per share, including $35 to shareholders, $4 in employee compensation and another $10 related to FIMI.

Yet public shareholders would receive only $35.

$ZIM has one of the youngest fleets in the industry. New ships can take three to four years to deliver. If Hapag-Lloyd is willing to commit approximately $49 per share, we believe it sees strategic value closer to $70.

And since the deal was announced, shipping rates have increased significantly, potentially making $ZIM even more valuable.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐬

The agreement restricts special dividends and buybacks while the deal remains pending. Hapag-Lloyd hoped to close before year-end, potentially acquiring $ZIM before its 2026 earnings were distributed.

Given the regulatory obstacles, we do not expect the deal to close before year-end.
We estimate 2026 earnings of approximately $12 per share, with oil prices potentially moving that figure by around $2 in either direction.

Our base-case dividends:

November 2026: ~$1.50/share
March 2027: ~$4.25/share
Total: 𝟓.𝟕𝟓/𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞, 𝐚 𝟐𝟎.𝟐% 𝐲𝐢𝐞𝐥𝐝.

If the deal collapses, we expect further substantial dividends and buybacks. This view also reflects conversations hedge funds are having with the company.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐁𝐚𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐒𝐡𝐞𝐞𝐭

At $28.50, $ZIM trades below our estimate of year-end cash of $32 per share, before the expected distributions.
Even after paying $5.75 in dividends, approximately $26.25 per share in cash would remain, assuming no other changes.

Most of $ZIM’s reported debt consists of lease liabilities. As of June 30, it had approximately $5.2 billion in lease liabilities versus only $80 million in loans and other liabilities. Many charter contracts were signed at highly attractive rates. Looking only at their liabilities while ignoring their economic value is misleading.

Think of renting a highly profitable taxi. The rental obligations are real, but what matters is the cash generated after paying them.

We estimate $ZIM could potentially restructure or exit some of its less profitable charter contracts and unlock another one billion in cash and economic value.

𝐁𝐨𝐧𝐮𝐬: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐇𝐢𝐝𝐝𝐞𝐧 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬

$ZIM recorded a substantial impairment in 2023 when the Harpex Index was around 700. Today it is near 2,500. A further reversal could potentially add approximately $3 per share in accounting earnings, although this would not itself generate cash.

Under our optimistic scenario, dividends through March could reach $7.50 per share, a 26.3% yield, subject to distributable profits and board approval.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐁𝐨𝐭𝐭𝐨𝐦 𝐋𝐢𝐧𝐞

We believe $ZIM offers one of the largest margins of safety in the market today, with substantial cash, valuable assets and extraordinary dividend potential.

We don’t need Hapag-Lloyd to buy the company. In fact, we would prefer it doesn’t.

𝐎𝐰𝐧 𝐢𝐭. 𝐂𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐬. 𝐋𝐞𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐮𝐬.

How I Trade $ZIM: 

My $ZIM position fluctuates between 5% and 30% of my portfolio. I hold $ZIM as a safe harbor because I currently consider it my safest position. If the market falls sharply and $ZIM holds its value, I sell part of my position to buy strong companies that have fallen hard. If the market goes up or stays flat, I simply keep my $ZIM position. I do trade in and out of positions, but not because I no longer believe in them. Sometimes you have to move from a good opportunity to an even better one. That’s what investing is all about, allocating capital where the best opportunities are, rather than falling in love with a stock.

I consider myself an imperfectionist. My memory is naturally wired for conceptual thinking rather than holding onto small details. Because of this, I focus on the big picture and how everything connects, which is exactly what being a global macro investor requires.

The greatest teacher I have found for this is simply taking action and learning from the results. In the markets, you get immediate, objective feedback. You can judge your performance down to three decimal places. When you are wrong, it hurts, and when you are right, it is rewarding. Relying on that constant feedback loop is the ultimate education.
#RayDalio #Principles

tweets.text:
the last 2 gens of bambulabs/most other 3d printer companies innovations have been more like going from a yacht to a slightly bigger yacht

way more expensive, functionally doesn't actually do that much more in terms of what you can actually do with it compared to prior gens, but looks (and honestly is) just a really cool toy

to give an example of what i mean, the biggest marketing angle they go for nowadays is still less filament waste, which is wild since you'd need 100s of kgs of spools worth of printing before cost of filament (ignoring the fact filament recycling getting far more accesible now) even comes close to the cost of the device itself

multihead multicolor printing is attainable at far cheaper costs

tl;dr is its very expensive and doesn't do anything unique, but if u think 3d printing is cool and have fun cool ideas and dont want to spend alot of time swapping out spools and fixing jams, it may be worth it to some

one of my largest mistakes this cycle was simply fitting a square peg into a round hole. there comes a point in every cycle where the trend clearly changed but each time investors will try to flip it bullish, and that point was clearest after leopold got liquidated

the bounce after that was the second top, the last chance to exit, but everyone was screaming how bulls are back and AI is a new paradigm. by then sentiment in the markets was clearly one of desperation and not a renewed sense of "climbing the wall of worry" - rather it was people justifying why their portfolios should make new highs 

it's funny because i used to always wonder how people did it, and then i did it myself. 

lesson in there.

tweets.text:
Quite frankly I think what we're seeing with software hacks and this AirBnB stuff is just the simple societal rule that every rule in society exists because of the bottom quintile

A small percentage of bad actors use AI much faster than good actors can catch up - and now airlines, fridges, electronics, databases and god knows how many old companies w outdated infra are just getting hacked

I feel like we're witnessing the collapse of software from a cultural perspective. I don't know about software stocks, but I can feel that people at the fringes just hate using software

The solution isn't "use AI to fight the AI hacks" because that doesn't take into account the fabric of human nature - the solution that people will opt for is instead a mass exodus out of software

Unironically the only thing AI might have killed is the very thing that built it. We're basically reverting back to 2010s era type of stuff - IRL meetups, only booking hotels, etc. 

I think the conclusion of "oh but better software will be built" is just not intuitive because there are just a myriad of vectors beyond traditional software - like look at Binance social engineering hack. It was, at the end of the day, not a cyber-hack but a social engineering that could have only been done at scale using AI - imagine just some guy deploying 100 agents of a female and it's just a numbers game before one gets hit

It is what it is.

tweets.text:
running a company nowadays feels kinda dystopian

my team is 50+ people in 12 countries, but i talk to my agents more than my human teammates

- voice note to grokbot
- mattpocock/skills /grill-me so the agent interrogates the idea before anything gets built
- spec drops into linear through the linear mcp
- exa + firecrawl agent reads every competitor site, pricing page and changelog
- https://t.co/a5ARFnvSnA to find ideas and trends
- apify pulls g2, reddit and app store reviews
- prompt: "find the 10 complaints that show up most and quote the users"
- context7 so the agent reads the latest docs before it touches any api

the design

- claude code + paper mcp
- 4 versions of every screen before a single line of code
- pick pieces from 2, it merges them. diverge then converge
- frontend-design skill from anthropic/skills + our own design system skill
- cleanshot screenshots of any ui i like go straight in with "make it feel like this"

the build

- pingdotgg/t3code as the control surface for every agent, from my phone too
- stablyai/orca runs a fleet of agents in parallel, each in its own git worktree
- graphify maps the whole codebase into a knowledge graph so agents navigate instead of guess
- headroom compresses tool outputs before they hit the model, so tokens go 20-95% further
- lsp plugins so the agent sees types and errors like an ide does
- security guidance hook flags risky edits before they land
- supabase mcp for the database, stripe for billing
- github mcp opens the pr, vercel spins up a preview
- loops run overnight, i check what shipped over coffee

the user testing

- lightpanda as the headless browser, way lighter than chromium so you can run hundreds at once
- agents click every flow on the preview like a first-time user
- one persona is impatient, one is confused, one is on a phone
- playwright + chrome devtools mcp for regression tests

the bugs

- sentry mcp catches the error
- agent reads the stack trace and opens a fix pr in under 10 minutes
- human just approves

the data

- posthog mcp cron at 7am on yesterday's funnel
- any step that drops more than 10%, the agent watches 20 session replays and tells me why
- stripe mcp pulls every cancellation reason into one doc every monday

the agents' tools

- orgo so every agent gets its own computer
- agentmail so every agent gets its own inbox
- agentphone so i can call them from the car
- composio connect-apps for every other connector
- akitaonrails/ai-memory, a git-backed markdown wiki so they remember what we decided last week

the skills

- wshobson/agents so skills work across claude code, codex and opencode
- my writing voice
- our design system
- how we write specs
- skill creator so the agents write new skills themselves

some helpful tricks

- one agent per platform. the x agent never touches email
- cheap model for triage, opus for anything that ships
- every output gets scored 1-10 by an llm judge. under 8 goes back
- every agent writes a 5-line log at night so i can read the whole company in 2 minutes
- every agent mistake becomes a new skill, so it only happens once

the team

- humans get version 5, not my voice note which they are happy about lol 
- their job is creative feedback, relationships and telling the agents what they got wrong

a human pm reviews the funnel once a week. this reviews it every morning

running a company is now voice notes and inference

The first day interning in finance you learn that models are only as good as their assumptions and garbage-in garbage-out.  

Polling as a profession attempts to calibrate their models based on assumptions about underlying sub-groups which are then calibrated from race to race and then ultimately tallied based on actual surveys.  

Like in finance where your model is great for predicting continuous events (change in top line or EPS trajectory quarter to quarter) but are terrible for predicting discontinuous events (Putin invades Ukraine, Russian bank nukes to zero) or events out of sample (company gets acquired, CEO sleeps with secretary) the polls are completely out of sample for MAGA because the correlation between people who don’t trust institutions, dont trust polsters enough to respond, and are likely to vote or turnout correlates strongly.  

And not only does it correlate strongly the correlation and overlap between those three groups are accelerating at the rate of deterioration of trust.  

I can wax philosophic all day about upward convexity on turnout due to gerrymandering and the inability to apply a Bayesian statistical approach to MAGA turnout but instead I’ll simplify it by saying the American populace is uniquely and viscerally averse to the values being propagated by the Dems and are increasingly immune to the false characterization attempted by the MSM. 

If you think red sweep today is bad just wait for the crimson bloodbath in 2029 when AI drives massive improvements to American quality of life as we weaponize hegemony and access to compute.  

🫡

Polling as a profession attempts to calibrate their models based on assumptions about underlying sub-groups which are then calibrated from race to race and then ultimately tallied based on actual surveys.  

Like in finance where your model is great for predicting continuous events (change in top line or EPS trajectory quarter to quarter) but are terrible for predicting discontinuous events (Putin invades Ukraine, Russian bank nukes to zero) or events out of sample (company gets acquired, CEO sleeps with secretary) the polls are completely out of sample for MAGA because the correlation between people who don’t trust institutions, dont trust polsters enough to respond, and are likely to vote or turnout correlates strongly.  

And not only does it correlate strongly the correlation and overlap between those three groups are accelerating at the rate of deterioration of trust.  

I can wax philosophic all day about upward convexity on turnout due to gerrymandering and the inability to apply a Bayesian statistical approach to MAGA turnout but instead I’ll simplify it by saying the American populace is uniquely and viscerally averse to the values being propagated by the Dems and are increasingly immune to the false characterization attempted by the MSM. 

If you think red sweep today is bad just wait for the crimson bloodbath in 2029 when AI drives massive improvements to American quality of life as we weaponize hegemony and access to compute.  

🫡

$PLTR 

Palantir TCV concerns are absolutely silly and the bears are becoming desperate.

First, every analyst on the street increased their PTs. You usually don't have analysts, that react to price movements, increase their targets when the stock is going against their bullish call. This quarter was SO good that every single one of them ignored what the stock was doing and told their clients that they think it's going higher.

Even Rishi from RBC (Motel 6) had to FINALLY raise his target into the $100s, upgrading Palantir from $90 to $130. You know the numbers were that good when Rishi has to upgrade by $40.

Second, this 6% TCV YoY growth completely misses what management said during the call. 

"We signed multiple 8-figure deals in the quarter that were shorter in duration than usual, as customers rapidly adopted initial Sovereign AI capabilities in their enterprise," noted CFO David Glazer.

This also explains why RPO was flat QoQ:

"As a reminder, RPO is primarily comprised of our commercial business, as it does not take into account contracts with an initial term of less than 12 months and contractual obligations that fall beyond termination for convenience clauses, both of which are common in most of our government business."

I mean the bears have really lost their minds to interpret low TCV and RPO growth as a reason why this quarter was bad. What Palantir is actually saying is they are signing customers that want to get started with deploying Sovereign AI ASAP. That means to get a shorter contract signed so the work can begin and as the value is created, those 8-figure deals can begin to expand out many years...because Palantir is not one of those companies that will get paid and deliver nothing. If anything, I see it as a sign of incredible strength that management is willing to sign contracts on a shorter term basis and immediately begin proving how transformational the Sovereign movement can become and earn their ability to extend those contracts. The fact that the top average revenue per top 20 customer is up from $83M a year to $146M a year, +76% YoY, shows how much value this company is creating and why net dollar retention is now 165%.

Customer count at 1090 customers is EXCITING, not a red flag, this is a company that is growing FASTER and more efficiently than any other software company on the planet, and doing so with less than 1100 customers...you would have to genuinely be desperate to think that that is bearish when in reality that means the relationships they have with their partners are truly transformational and they aren't just signing customers to sign them but rather every time they get someone in the door, they can keep them for a VERY long time and monetize that relationship better than any other software company because that customer is actually receiving the value they pay for. 

Bears, you need a better bear case to take down one of the single greatest companies the market has ever seen. 

Please, try harder.
